caption_text: Total Control Advanced Riding Clinics are utilized extensively by the U.S. military to reduce mishaps (injuries and fatalities). Here Total Control students at Langley Air Force Base in Virginia pose with a Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor after class.

The author started racing professionally in 1994 where he finished second overall in the AMA Superbike Championship in the 125 GP class (now called Moto 3). It was during this time that he began his intellectual journey into figuring out the physical, mental, and mechanical dynamics of riding faster and safer.
Getting coaching from our professional instructors is the most effective way to put Total Control techniques into practice. Use this book as the gateway to taking your riding to another level.

After retiring from professional road racing at the end of 2001, the author made a one-time appearance in the Triumph Thruxton Cup Challenge national series at Willow Springs Raceway in 2005. Using the techniques in this book, he won the race on a virtually stock motorcycle, beating many notable regulars including three-time Grand National Champion Jay “Springer” Springsteen.

Having an accurate tire gauge, like this one manufactured domestically by Lee Parks Design, is critical to proper tire life and traction. This particular gauge is hand tested to be within +/- 1 lb. and has information on reading dates codes on the sidewall of the tire printed on it. While dial gauges can be very accurate, they can also be easily thrown out of adjustment if they are dropped or bumped around in a toolbox. To see if your gauges are accurate, bring them to the races and ask one of the race tire vendors to check it against theirs, which are regularly calibrated and stored in protective cases.

Racers and track day riders use tire warmers like these from Chicken Hawk Racing to “preheat” their tires before heading out on the track. This is because racing tires are designed to work at extremely high temperatures and they can actually have less traction than street tires at lower temperatures.

Gaining popularity these days are multiple compound tires. These “best-of-both-worlds” designs use a harder compound in the middle for better mileage and softer compounds on the edges for maximum grip at high lean angles.
Here’s how to “crack the code” of all those numbers and letters on your tire’s sidewall. Most importantly, the last four digits in the oval represent when the tire was manufactured.
The only thing that is missing from the tire size code is the rim width, and that is critical information.

An all-too-common problem with tire sizing is knowing what rim width is appropriate. In the example above, rider Frank on his SV650 is achieving impressive lean angles with a stock-sized 160/60VR17 tire mounted on the rear. Or is it? This particular tire was sold by a reputable company, but the employees didn’t realize it was designed specifically for a 5.0 inch rim. When put on the 4.5 inch stock rim, it became so pinched that the “chicken strips,” the part of the tire that hasn’t been used yet, were angled to the point where the bike would literally have to be crashed for them to touch the ground. This means that at the point of maximum lean, the contact patch becomes dangerously small. See Figure 1.5.

Notice how the same tire on three different rim widths has very different sized contact patches. On a too-narrow rim (top) only part of the tire’s width can be effectively used and the contact patch shrinks. The correct rim size (middle) maximizes the size and placement of the contact patch resulting in the most traction possible. A too-wide rim (bottom) forces the contact patch to be tiny at high lean angles and may prevent the tire’s bead from properly seating, possibly causing slippage or air leakage. For the same reasons, automotive tires should never be used on two- or three-wheeled motorcycles that lean.

Tire profiles can significantly alter the way your bike handles. Shown are two current Bridgestone DOT racing tires (R10R on the left and 003R on the right) with rounded and triangular profiles, respectively. Racers choose the best shape for them depending on the bike they are on or the track they are at.

Three different types of tires have unique tread patterns. Sportbike tires (left) have minimal tread for optimum traction at the limit on dry days. Dual-sport tires have large groves in them to help “bite” into dirt (middle). Touring tires have lots of tread to help displace water and other debris on the road in adverse conditions.
Tread in a tire allows the rubber to cut through water and small debris on the road. Racing “slicks” begin to aquaplane on top of the water, which is why they are used only in dry conditions.
The three basic forces we put into a bike are always trying to use up the finite amount of traction available. Learning how to balance them is key to achieving Total Control.

Wider tires have a much larger “lever effect” on the steering when hitting rocks or other obstacles than narrow tires, causing unwanted directional changes. This is part of why front tires are narrower than rear tires and why off-road bikes use narrower tires than their on-road counterparts.
Wider tires require more lean angle for the same speed than narrower tires due to the contact patch offset from the bike’s centerline.

The higher the bike’s CG the less lean angle is needed due to the contact patch offset from the bike’s centerline. Narrower tires with a smaller contact patch offset have less of a lean-angle effect from CG height changes.

The farther you can move your body to the inside of the turn, the less lean angle is needed for a given speed and radius. Once you find the correct combined center of gravity (CG) of the rider and machine, virtually no steering effort is required on the bars to maintain a given line. The picture was taken during a wet race at Summit Point, WV with three riders on SV650s going through a similar arc at a similar speed. Notice how the author’s bike (#311) is leaned over less than the other two due to a combined CG that is closer to the inside of the turn. This allows for earlier and harder application of the throttle on the exit and greater ground clearance.

Countersteering, or a quick steering input counter to the direction you want to go, is the primary action that causes the bike to begin leaning into the turn. This happens because the front and rear wheels are temporarily facing in different directions, which unbalances the bike causing it to begin falling. Once that happens, the castor effect of the trail causes the front tire to steer into the turn and maintain a clean line. After the bike is in the turn, slow direct-steering movements can be used to tighten or widen the line. The rate of change of the steering inputs determines if the result will be direct steering (slow) or countersteering (quick).

Motorcycle simulators have been tried in various forms and levels of sophistication. They can be very useful for body position training but none have been able to accurately simulate the effects of steering as of this writing. The most sophisticated version used by the author (upper left) has been tried in the armed forces without much success. While it does a decent job simulating accelerating, braking, and shifting, its steering process is not even remotely accurate, and can have the effect of teaching bad muscle memory to new riders before they even get on a real bike for the first time.

In the perfect world, the center of gravity of the sprung mass doesn’t move vertically. The wheel remains in contact with the ground at all times. This can only be achieved with active suspension where the wheel is sucked up on the face of the bump and pushed down on the back side. The technology to do this is not here yet, but this is the ideal ultimate goal.
Most bikes use one of three basic types of springs. From left to right: straight-rate, dual-rate and true progressive-rate springs.
One way spring rate can be calculated is by applying a known amount of force and then dividing that amount by the distance the spring travels.

This is a force-deflection curve for two different stiffness springs. The blue spring requires .5 kg additional force for each 10mm increment through its entire range. The red spring is twice as stiff, so it has twice the slope, requiring an additional 1.0 kg for each 10mm increment.
An accurate spring tester can be an invaluable tool for suspension tuners. This Intercomp basic unit will test only rear springs. A fork spring tester kit can be added on to this basic unit as well.

Progressive springs gradually increase force through their travel, while dual-rate springs have a distinct “crossover point” where they change rates. Straight-rate springs have a constant spring rate.
The total spring force is a combination of mechanical spring and air spring.

This graph shows the difference between adding preload to a softer spring (blue line) compared to a stiffer rate spring (red line) with less preload. Notice that the two lines cross at the 30 mm fork travel mark. This means that both of these setups have the same amount of static sag, which demonstrates that there is much more to spring choice than just sag. The stiffer spring with less preload is a better choice if the rider is experiencing bottoming out with the alternative setup. On the other hand, if the rider is not generally using all of the available travel, the softer spring with more preload is preferable for a plusher ride.

This figure shows the relationship between spring preload and sag. It also illustrates how changing preload changes the percentage of the suspension’s travel that is available for compression and extension.
Use this chart to determine what rate fork springs you should have in your bike for optimum handling. It works with any brand of fork spring. Courtesy of RaceTech.

Larger sport-tourers and dressers can have serious weight differentials based on passengers and luggage. Having the correct spring rate for the load is the single most important aspect of your suspension.

This shows the relationship between rebound damping and traction, control, and plushness. Note that when traction is falling off as rebound is increased, the feeling of control is still increasing. Most riders will benefit from using less rebound damping than they are used to. Rebound damping is approximately three times stronger than compression damping. This is because it must control the releasing of stored energy of the spring, which unloads all of its energy at once. The ideal range of settings that fall into the “just right” Goldilocks Zone is therefore quite limited, making accurate rebound settings critical for good traction.

Notice that, as with rebound damping, both traction and control drop off as compression damping is increased. It doesn’t fall off as rapidly as with rebound. Notice also that the peak for control is to the right of traction once again. The range of settings that fall into the “just right” Goldilocks Zone is significantly larger than for rebound damping. This is because we are dealing with a significantly reduced force compared to rebound damping as the springs do most of the work absorbing bump energy.
Suspension damping clickers are fragile, and should not be forced when counting clicks. Even though the slots are large, they should only be turned by hand with a small screwdriver.
Professional suspension tuners and manufacturers use precise tools to test their components. A shock dyno takes a lot of the guesswork out of performance analysis.
BMW’s US GS Trophy Team member, Bill Dragoo is about to experience first-hand the importance of correct spring rates and compression damping.

Fear is a necessary evil for self-preservation, but experienced riders are able to keep it in check by building their confidence level. A paradigm shift is a change from one way of thinking to another. It’s a transformation driven by agents of change. To progress from a mental state of fear to confidence, the agents of change are knowledge and faith.

Few things strike fear into the hearts of professional racers like the threat of an oily track. Here a giant turbine blows the oil dry off Daytona International Speedway as part of a crash cleanup. Every racer will have to decide how much faith he has in the condition of the track, as well as his tires, when the green flag drops again. Those who have faith, tempered with the knowledge of previous similar experiences, hold a serious advantage.
Improv artists never let anything faze them. Using their secret of “accepting everything at face value” can help keep riders safe on the road when the unexpected happens.
In a perceived emergency your body is programmed to “go with what you know.” If you’ve not practiced riding with a little bit of fear, you will likely panic when subjected to an unexpected event.

Even a moment’s lapse of concentration can have disastrous results. Pictured is the unconscious author, moments after crashing in his first supermoto race in 2004. It happened after crossing the finish line when he was no longer paying close attention to the rider ahead and was not ready for him to hit the brakes. Seventeen minutes later he regained consciousness and immediately screamed out, “Don’t cut off my leathers!” At that point he realized he was now wearing a neck brace and not much else.

Distracted and inattentive motorcycle operation is becoming one of the biggest concerns of the National Traffic Highway Safety Administration (NHTSA). This photo is of the author after 975 miles and 22 straight hours of riding taken by Iron Butt Association President Mike Kneebone. Realizing that he was now a danger to himself and other motorists due to fatigue, Parks took a one-hour “Iron Butt Motel” to get some rest. This left him just refreshed enough to finish up the last 45 miles to the finish line for his first (and last!) Saddlesore 1000.

Honda’s latest Asimo (Advanced Step in Innovative Mobility) robot debuted in 2005 and can walk, run (3.7 mph), and turn. For slalom running at 3.1 mph, the center of gravity is moved toward the direction of the turn before the actual turning takes place—just like Step 2 in the 10 Steps to Proper Cornering (see Chapter 12: Body Positioning).

Retrospective analysis of your experience will help hone your concentration when you ride. If you go riding with a buddy, talk about what hazards each of you noticed during the ride when you stop for a break. This is a great opportunity to see what each of you paid attention to, and which things you missed that you want to be on the lookout for the next time.

The mind can only handle up to seven issues at one time. Being able to discern what’s important from what isn’t is critical in high performance situations. In the corkscrew at Laguna Seca, riders must deal with directional, speed, and elevation changes, while simultaneously monitoring their bike’s systems and the other riders’ actions. It is as much a mental workout as a physical one.

Having the wrong attitude can lead to bad choices. Bad choices can include treating public roads like a racetrack. Treating public roads like a racetrack can lead to uncomfortable bracelets. Don’t end up with uncomfortable bracelets. Practice Total Control techniques and achieve the right attitude.

Olympic athletes and professional racers alike use visualization training to help learn new skills and develop consistency. When it comes to learning, the human mind doesn’t differentiate between real and imagined experiences. When it comes to physical pain, however, the human body definitely does!
Overconfidence can turn into recklessness on the street or the track. Even when you (or another rider) make a mistake, the right attitude can transform it into a learning experience.
Looking all the way through the corner allows a much better line choice. To make vision easier it helps to turn your shoulders into the turn, as well.
Looking at the ground in front of you increases your sense of speed. Using floodlight vision and looking farther ahead decreases your sense of speed and helps keep your mind and body relaxed.

Practice riding in a circle and looking through the turn to the exit on the opposite side. Have a friend stand in the middle and see if your eyes are dancing around or staying focused on the constantly moving exit.

The most common line selection mistake is turning too early. Not only does it restrict your ability to see around blind corners, but it forces you to run wide at the exit and limits what mid-corner corrections you can make.

Similar in its consequences to premature initiation, slow steering into a corner causes you to stay at maximum lean for an extended period of time. A quick steering input can get most of the turning done early in the corner, which allows for more line options at the exit.

The English 50-pence coin has a multi-faceted design, which is the inspiration for the multiple-turn-points line negatively referred to as “fifty pencing.” This particular coin is from the Isle of Man and celebrates the famed Isle of Man TT race.
Having multiple mid-corner steering corrections is the mark of a beginning rider or a badly misjudged corner. It is usually caused by not looking far enough through the turn.
Stayin’ Safe Advanced Rider Training’s Eric Trow teaches students about line selection in one of his “chalk talks.” On-street training is one of the best ways to learn safe riding strategies.

Racetrack-based training like the Total Control Track Clinic often uses cones to help riders pick good entry, apex, and exit points. This allows students to “connect the dots” for a perfect line every time. Here the apex of turn 10 at Horsethief Mile is designated by a cone featuring that number. Numbered cones help students remember particular points on the track when receiving feedback from the instructors.

The dreaded decreasing radius turn can bite even an experienced rider if he didn’t have plenty of lean angle in reserve. With a delayed entry, it can be safely completed with only one turning point. In the case of blind corners, if you don’t know if it is a decreasing radius, you can take either path shown but at a significantly lower speed.

Corners that require two or more apexes to navigate come in many shapes and sizes. The key is to plan as far ahead as possible in picking your turn points, before necessity forces them on you when you least expect it.
Multiple linked turns can be the most challenging for line selection because you have to think more than one turn ahead. A mistake on the initial turn gets amplified with each successive turn.

Choosing a proper line requires mental preparation and a good view of where you’re about to turn. While it can be scary to be close to the outside of the road so deep into a turn, the resulting line provides a much greater safety margin overall.

Former World Superbike and 250 GP Champion John Kocinski was famous for his masterful throttle control. His touch was so deft, in fact, that he was able to run markedly more compliant suspension settings than other riders his weight because he didn’t upset the chassis with excessive throttle movements.

This illustration depicts a high-speed turn where the rider is doing a lot of trail braking (see Chapter 11: Braking) upon entry. Notice how rapidly the bike gets leaned over and how the throttle is being applied before the brakes are completely released. This helps minimize the weight transfer to the rear, which keeps the suspension balanced for better traction during acceleration. As you can see the application of throttle is inversely proportional to lean angle on exit.

Unlike the days of manually changing carburetor jets for the best throttle response, fuel injection tuning is now done on dynamometers with computer software changes. Pictured is a Bazzaz Principia dyno being used to set up the fuel map for a GSX-R1000. The top of the line system uses the same controller for the fuel map, quick-shifter and traction control.

Traction control can be a tremendous confidence booster on a motorcycle and is coming stock on more bikes these days. Some companies like Bazzaz offer it as an aftermarket upgrade. Pictured (top) is a screen shot of the Bazzaz software that allows the user to program each gear and rpm range with varying amounts of traction control depending on conditions. An optional rotary dial (below) allows easy external adjustments to the system while riding. Note the attached fuel map switch to the right of the dial. It can have two pre-programmed settings for, say, performance and fuel economy.

Racing two-stroke 125 GP bikes taught the author the importance of quick shifts and proper gear selection. With less than 45 hp and a razor-thin powerband, racers must constantly row up and down the six gears to keep the bike in the 1,500-rpm “money-making” range.

Preloading the shift lever with your foot will significantly reduce the time required to shift. On the track that means faster lap times. On the street it means easier transitions between gears for a smoother ride.

Comparing the speed over time on a GSX-R600 with conventional shifting (blue) vs. an electronic quick-shifter (red) is astonishing. Because the shifts happen so fast, the dyno software doesn’t show the minute change in speed during the shift except under very high magnification. Using the clutchless upshifting technique yields a result closer to the red line.

More bikes like this Triumph Jason Disalvo Daytona 675 Race Replica are starting to come with quick-shifters. They detect movement in the shift linkage and cut the ignition for approximately 50 milliseconds to allow for full and partial throttle upshifts without use of the clutch.
Quick, precise shifts will be especially valued by passengers. You’ll also appreciate not getting bonked in the back of the head.

There are two parts necessary to downshift properly. The first one is complicated. And the second one is more complicated! In Part 1, you want to simultaneously roll off the throttle and apply the front brake. Part 2 has us simultaneously maintaining even pressure on the brake while we quickly roll on and off the throttle, quickly engage and disengage the clutch, while at the same time quickly downshifting.

In a 2001 road race at Summit Point Raceway, the author gets a holeshot from all the way in the back row of the lightweight class. Effective clutch use with quick shifts was worth more than raw horsepower as several of the bikes pictured had as much as a 10–20-hp advantage over the #311 SV650.

Few things scare riders like hard braking in the wet. In racing circles rain is known as the “great equalizer,” as horsepower and braking power must be used judiciously. While rain tires help provide traction, even MotoGP champions like Valentino Rossi can’t break the laws of physics.

One of the most debated topics in rider training is whether you should use two or four fingers during braking. The correct answer is whichever way you’re more comfortable—but know the tradeoffs. Most modern sportbikes can stand up on the front wheel with only two fingers. Many cruisers and tourers with inefficient brakes require a lot of pressure on the front lever to do an adequate amount of braking. The more fingers on the brakes, the less steering and throttle control is available. The fewer fingers on the brakes, the less power is available at the lever.
The rear brake is especially effective at low speeds for trail braking. At higher speeds it can reduce the amount of weight transfer to the front tire when used along with the front brake.

Racetracks will often have cone brake markers at the end of the straights labeled 3, 2, and 1 to provide riders with reference points for when to begin braking. Being aware of your relationship to them can help build consistency and allow for methodological improvement.

Braking trainers like Skidbike (skidbike.com) are a great way to practice front wheel lockups without the physical pain usually associated with failure. Skidbikes allow the rider to precisely adjust the traction conditions from rain to snow.
Trail braking can be done with the front (shown), rear, or both brakes. The faster you go, the more effective front trail braking is—the slower you go, the more you should favor rear trail braking.

The dreaded front wheel lockup! It leaves a path of dark rubber right before the bike falls down … or the rider releases the brakes for an instant to let the tire regain traction and reapplies the brakes.
In road racing sometimes form has to be balanced with aerodynamics. Here World Superbike racer Jules Cluzel tries to split the difference in turn 3 at Mazda Raceway Laguna Seca.

You will know when you get the right body position because the bike will go around corners easily with virtually no steering effort on the grips. On race-replicas your outside arm should lightly rest on the tank with your inside foot, outside leg, and core holding up the majority of your weight—not your arms.

While it is important to be relaxed on the bike, you don’t want to end up getting lazy and simply pushing the bike underneath you. When that happens it is easy to run out of ground clearance and therefore, grip.

Even in full rain conditions on a large sport-tourer, proper body position with a relaxed hold on the bike can allow for some serious lean angles. Total Control instructor Rob “Birdman” Hephner demonstrates.

Biologically speaking, human beings are predators. As carnivores, specifically, we are genetically predisposed to going after our prey in the direction of our head, shoulders, and hips. This means you want all three of their axes facing toward the exit of the corner (“The Doctor” demonstrates). If you start twisting them out of alignment to one another, your nervous system can send confusing signals to the brain about where it is going, making proper muscle inputs more difficult to execute.

Motocross racers like Ricky Carmichael use the opposite body position as street riding and road racing. On a dirt bike, the rider pushes the bike underneath him, instead of leaning with the bike. Because the bikes are so tall, the riders are able to trade some of their ample ground clearance for better control while sliding. This way the rear end of the bike can move independently from the rider like a pendulum to find traction, but without the added inertia of the rider’s weight.

Read left-to-right, this figure shows the relative position of each of the 10 Steps to Proper Cornering in a typical constant radius corner. Notice that steps 2 and 3, and steps 6 and 7 are performed simultaneously, regardless of their relationship to the other steps.

Even heavy, full-dress tourers can make almost effortless tight turns with the proper technique. While not visible here, the rider’s inside foot is literally dangling as the majority of his weight sits on the outside peg.

Quinn Redeker, from the Ventura Police Department, is one of the best tight turners in the country. He regularly dominates competitions against other motor officers because he utilizes skills learned from trials to road racing. Quinn has been nicknamed “The Owl” for his incredible head-turning capability. “Tradition” is the lame reason given by motor officers for not wearing protective jackets during competition. Auxiliary lights, like these trick Clearwater units (www.clearwaterlights.com), are a popular modification for long-distance riding, as well as for motor officers.

Super-passenger Pricilla Wong says the most important factors in high-performance passengering are “complete trust in the rider” and “keeping an eye on what’s next to avoid surprises.” Keeping your hands in front of the rider is ideal for hard acceleration.

When boarding, swinging the right leg over the seat is the least taxing on the rider. If that is not possible, the rider should counter the passenger’s weight by leaning the bike slightly away from her as she puts her left foot on the left peg, stands up and swings the right leg over the bike. By leaning forward the rider makes it easier for the passenger to climb on the bike. The passenger should never put her feet down again until it’s time to get off the bike.

During braking, if you can’t reach around the rider and use the tank as a brace, there are several other acceptable alternatives for your hands: Holding the grab rail (above), placing your hands on the rider’s lower back, or holding the rider’s waist (following images).

Three popular rear suspension preload adjusters include hydraulic hand knobs (top), threaded collars (middle), and ramped collars (bottom). Rear rebound damping adjusters are usually found at the bottom of shocks with compression damping on the top. Check your owner’s manual to see what adjustments you have on your bike.

Some front forks utilize novel adjusting mechanisms. A Jason DiSalvo Replica Triumph Daytona 675 (top) uses a triangular preload attachment for tool-less hand adjustments. The BMW S1000RR’s rebound damping settings are labeled from 1 to 10 and can be adjusted with the stock screwdriver-shaped ignition key.

Most cartridge forks have the rebound damping adjuster on the fork cap that can be adjusted with a small screwdriver. It will often be labeled with the letters “TEN” (tension) “R”, or “REB” (rebound). A few models, such as this 2010 Yamaha R1, newer FZ1s, many Moto Guzzis, and some others have one fork cap for compression labeled with a “COMP” or “C” (left cap) and the other for rebound (right cap). The preload is generally adjusted with a 12 to 14mm wrench.

Steering dampers, like this trick rotary unit from GPR (gprstabilizer.com), can help minimize headshake when bikes are ridden at the limit. Keep in mind that if your bike needs a steering damper to handle properly at street speeds, you probably have a suspension, misalignment, or geometry issue that needs to be addressed.

Meet the motorcycle chiropractors—Scheibner Mega-M.A.X. (top) and G.M.D. Computrack (bottom). These competing chassis optimization companies diagnose handling problems and can make any bike corner like a pro’s. Keep in mind the problem may turn out to be the seat/handlebar interface!

More sportbikes like this Triumph 675 are starting to come with replaceable swingarm pivots to adjust anti-squat. On this particular bike, the original pivot point was a few mm below the center point. Now it’s a few mm above center for less squat under hard acceleration.

These custom adjustable triple clamps use interchangeable aluminum inserts that fit into the oval shaped hole. Changing the position of the steering stem directly changes the trail without affecting the rake.

15mm taller fork caps manufactured by Race Tech, combined with a 4mm internal increase in fork length, increased trail from 92mm to 97mm on the author’s Triumph Street Triple R. This significantly increased stability for aggressive street riding, but for track riding even more trail was added with the custom triple clamps shown.

G.M.D. Computrack’s Trackmotion is a new inertia motion data recording technology. It samples 100 times per second on six discrete channels. All the turning and acceleration motions of a ride are recorded on a specially mounted iPhone. This allows you to compare the performance of different riders and bikes around a course. Both riding style and bike handling can be analyzed to discover problems and recommend improvements. Check out totalcontroltraining.net to see when it will be available in your area.

A wide concave-shaped seat on a Ducati 999 distributes pressure evenly across the surface area of the rider’s butt. The narrow gas tank not only allows the legs to be in a more comfortable position, but it also provides the rider’s body more leverage to transition the bike from side to side. As an added bonus, a narrow tank allows the legs to be held closer in, reducing frontal area and the resulting aerodynamic drag. A rubberized tank protector to prevent scratches is also a nice touch.
Zero Gravity makes optically clear sportbike windscreens in various heights and designs. They can significantly minimize rider fatigue on the street and the track.

Many sportbikes are quite uncomfortable for regular street use but Helibars (www.helibars.com) can help make the pain go away without compromising performance. For comparison, this Yamaha R1 is equipped with a Helibar on the left side and a stock unit on the right. The Helibars are taller, farther rearward, wider, and utilize all the stock cables for a simple bolt-on improvement. By adding more leverage, they actually make the bike easier to turn.

While many people think of cruisers as being comfortable bikes, oftentimes they can be the least comfortable on a long ride because of what happens to the rider’s spine. With the pictured rider’s feet forward—and the stock seat angle—his pelvis rotates back causing his spine to bend outward in Lumbar Kyphosis (above). This takes away the spine’s natural ability to absorb impacts and can become sore. Proper curvature of the lower back known as Lumbar Lordosis (next image), can be achieved by changing the angle of the seat and/or precise positioning of a backrest to rotate the pelvis forward.

Spider grips are probably the best compromise for grip, comfort, and vibration damping for sportbikes on the market today. They provide an ideal amount of friction with your gloves to allow a loose grip for better feel, and help prevent cramping.

Because no control setup will fit all riders or conditions, some bikes like this Ducati 999 (above) have adjustable controls. In this case the footpeg bracket can be located using several different sets of mounting holes, while the brake lever uses a sliding mount. Unfortunately, this bike comes with extremely slippery footpegs. By contrast, the Aprilia Mille (next image) has been outfitted with Woodcraft Technologies’ (www.woodcraft-cfm.com) rearsets and footpegs that have an aggressive knurling pattern that allows boots to stay in place under hard cornering. Note how the peg has a breakaway design that allows the outside part of the peg to come off in a crash but still be rideable with the remaining stub.

This adjustable shift lever (www.touratech-usa.com) is able to keep the control within foot’s reach of a 4 foot 11 inch rider. As shown, an extra sole was also added to her boots to help her reach the ground on a BMW G650GS.

One of the easiest improvements you can make to the ergonomics of a motorcycle is to adjust the angle of the levers. Ideally, the rider’s wrist should be as straight as possible. With so many small wrist bones, even a slight incline can translate into pain on a long ride.

The brake and clutch controls should not be set up so the rider has to take his hand off the grip to partially curl his fingers around the levers (above). By adjusting the position closer (next image) the rider’s fingers have a comfortable reach to the levers and can simultaneously maintain good steering control.

No matter what kind of seat you have, you can make it more comfortable with an aftermarket pad. There are many different types available made with everything from sheepskin to wooden beads. They work by distributing the weight over a larger surface area. The most effective models utilize an adjustable air bladder system like the one pictured (bottom) from AirHawk (www.airhawk.net). They employ the same technology as wheelchair cushions and bed-toppers in hospitals made for preventing bedsores. Pressure maps, like the ones adjacent, show the amount and distribution of pressure with a gel and memory foam pad (left) vs. an air bladder unit (right).

Tank grips, like this one from Tech-spec (techspec-usa.com) can make high-performance riding significantly easier. By adding a high-traction compound to the sides of the gas tank, the rider can hang off without sliding off the inside of the bike. This is especially important when wearing slippery textile pants, but works great with all sorts of riding gear. When decelerating the rider can likewise keep from sliding forward by squeezing his knees against the tank. This can significantly reduce upper body fatigue during hard braking.

The only way to get a seat with exactly the right height, shape, angle and distance for your body—and your pillion’s—is to get a custom made model. Pictured is Rick Mayer (www.rickmayercycle.com) seen creating the seat for the author’s Triumph Street Triple R. In addition to being an artisan seat maker who has personally ridden over 1,000,000 miles, Rick is a registered nurse with a keen understanding of physiology.
Tucking in behind a fairing is not a comfortable position to be in at low speeds but it makes a real difference in straight-line performance.

The use of aerodynamic humps on leathers is de riguer these days. They help fill in some of the low-pressure area behind the rider’s helmet and smooth the shape of the rider’s back. While they won’t add much, if any, top speed to the bike, they do minimize the amount of drag on the helmet, which can significantly reduce neck fatigue.

It’s virtually impossible to find a modern sportbike with an aerodynamic tail section. Shown from above is a 2003 Ducati 999 with rider aboard. As you can see on the rider’s left side, the tail is too narrow to keep the airflow attached, forming drag-inducing, turbulent “eddies.” The flat back, Kamm-style fix, as proposed on the opposite side in blue, follows the “7-degree rule” of converging at no more than 7 degrees per side to keep the air attached for minimum drag. This type of improvement made on both sides should provide a 2–5 mph increase in top speed. The under seat exhaust also helps fill in the low-pressure area behind the bike.

Aerodynamic testing is now able to be done on the computer. This image is a horizontal slice of the Erik Buell Racing (EBR) 1190RX with the rider at 100mph. The top view represents the flow velocities and pattern at that one 2-D plane shown by the line in the side view. EBR has been using the evolving versions of such software for a decade, and a few years ago reached the point where it is more accurate than a real wind tunnel, as it provides far more discreet data on what is affecting pressure and velocity, and is much faster.

The radical $35,000 Benelli Tornado minimizes cooling drag by positioning the radiator under the seat and ducting fresh air to it. When the bike is not moving, two fans under the taillight help keep things cool by creating a vacuum to suck air through the radiator.

Comparing the frontal areas on different bikes is easy. Simply take a picture of them from the front with an outfitted rider on board (to establish a constant scale for the photo, use the same focal length, same height and same distance to the subject), and lay graph paper on the photo. By counting the number of squares (including partial ones) that are covered by bike or rider, you can make an accurate comparison. While you can see Ducati did a pretty good job of keeping the rider out of the airstream on the 999, there is still room for improvement. The upper fairing should be wider and taller to cover the rider’s knee pucks, hands, and shoulders. Also the rear brake pedal should be farther inboard because it forces the rider’s toe into the airstream. A taller windscreen would also help reduce neck fatigue without adding frontal area.

Motorcycle racers are among the fittest of athletes due to the need for a combination of both fast-twitch (strength) and slow-twitch (endurance) muscle fibers. Wrestling a 250-hp rocketship in 100-plus-degree weather wearing a thick leather suit requires tremendous physical and mental stamina.
Multi-time 250GP national champion Rich Oliver trains his eyesight for better vision as well as hand-eye coordination. He also underwent corrective surgery to help optimize his situational awareness.
The best gear is transparent to the rider, effortlessly following his lead and never getting in the way. On a hot day, it doesn’t hurt to have a powered cooling system, either.

Street riding suits come in many styles and materials. Three of the author’s favorites are (from left to right): BMW TourShell (long-distance touring), Aerostich Transit 2 (daily commuting), and Klim Badlands (adventure-touring).

Total Control’s (totalcontroltraining.net) convenient Strap-Ons allow a rider to temporarily add knee pucks to any pants. They work with virtually any sliders and prevent leaks in waterproof pants by eliminating the need to sew through the material.

Custom-fitted suits like this one from Syed Leathers are often no more expensive than high-quality, off-the-rack suits, yet can provide a perfect fit. Buying a domestically manufactured suit makes getting repairs, alterations, and cleanings a lot faster and easier.

Good riding gloves should have extra protection in the high abrasion areas of the knuckles and palm, and have a retention strap to keep them on in a crash. All riding gear should have as few seams as possible to minimize the chances of them coming apart. The DeerSports gloves produced by the author (leeparksdesign.com) shown below, feature a seamless palm and only four seams in the entire glove, for superior structural integrity. The somewhat similar appearing pair of gloves shown above has some dark secrets under its patches. The top of the glove has two structural seams where the top layer was cut out and replaced with a foam-padded section. Under the palm patch is a large horizontal cut with the leather held together with tape and Kevlar thread.

Most premium racing boots offer great protection and ventilation but at the cost of comfort and waterproofness. Most touring boots have the opposite results. A few modern “crossover” boots like this SportDry model from BMW allow you to have footwear that is both protective and waterproof, but gets a little warm on hot days. Choose your compromise.

High-end helmets like the C3 Pro (left) and S2 (right) from Schuberth epitomize what you get for the extra money. This includes significantly less wind noise, lighter weight with better aerodynamics for less neck strain, pull-down sunshields for taming bright light, efficient ventilation for keeping cool in hot weather, optically clear shields for better vision and moisture wicking/washable/customizable liners. Comfort is based on personal head shapes so you must try on any helmet before purchasing one. Any proper fitting full-face or modular helmet that meets ECE and/or DOT standards will provide decent protection, regardless of price.
